L21@P0: The Communications System
L22@P0: for Advanced Automotive
L23@P0: Control Applications
L24@P0: The rapid growth in advanced automotive
L25@P0: control systems requires a new, more powerful
L26@P0: communications protocol to ensure a network
L27@P0: that works together to accomplish critical
L28@P0: tasks within the vehicle. The FlexRay™
L29@P0: Consortium—made up of a group of industry
L30@P0: heavyweights, including Freescale—formed
L31@P0: to enable the development of next-generation
L32@P0: by-wire systems and to promote an
L33@P0: open-source network communications protocol
L34@P0: for the automotive industry.
L35@P0: FlexRay founders Motorola (Freescale
L36@P0: Semiconductor), Philips, BMW and
L37@P0: DaimlerChrysler have been working together
L38@P0: since 2000 to help speed the adoption of the
L39@P0: FlexRay protocol, a communications protocol
L40@P0: designed to handle the growing number of
L41@P0: digital elements that make up a 21st century
L42@P0: automobile. Over the past two years, others,
L43@P0: including Bosch, General Motors, Ford,
L44@P0: Volkswagen and Siemens VDO, have joined
L45@P0: these leaders in an effort to make FlexRay the
L46@P0: de facto standard for advanced applications in
L47@P0: the automotive industry. As of August 2004,
L48@P0: more than 80 companies from the automotive,
L49@P0: semiconductor and software industries are
L50@P0: supporting the FlexRay standard. The goal is
L51@P0: for the first FlexRay enabled vehicles to hit the
L52@P0: street by model year 2006.
L53@P0: Systems Working Together
L54@P0: The FlexRay protocol is expected to be
L55@P0: a comprehensive communication system,
L56@P0: providing speed, flexibility and scalability
L57@P0: for complex networks. The protocol’s key
L58@P0: features include:
L59@P0: > Time- and event-triggered
L60@P0: communication schemes
L61@P0: > Support of fault-tolerant systems
L62@P0: > High error detection and error
L63@P0: diagnosis capability
L64@P0: > Support of different network topologies
L65@P0: for cost-effective and safety-enhanced
L66@P0: partitioning of the system
L67@P0: > Dedicated automotive electrical physical
L68@P0: layer with sophisticated powerdown
L69@P0: and wake up mechanisms
L70@P0: > Flexible extendability and full scalability
L71@P0: to enable upgrades
L72@P0: Among the applications that the FlexRay
L73@P0: protocol is expected to make possible are
L74@P0: x-by-wire systems such as brake-by-wire
L75@P0: and steer-by-wire. X-by-wire removes the
L76@P0: need for hydraulic and mechanical
L77@P0: systems, connecting the driver to these
L78@P0: systems using sophisticated electronic
L79@P0: systems that are less expensive to build
L80@P0: and easier to maintain.
L81@P0: Other applications that the FlexRay protocol
L82@P0: is expected to enable include active and
L83@P0: passive safety systems, collision avoidance
L84@P0: systems, powertrain management systems
L85@P0: and driver assistance systems. With a gross
L86@P0: data rate of 10 Mbits/sec, FlexRay delivers
L87@P0: approximately 20 times higher net bandwidth
L88@P0: than the CAN protocol currently
L89@P0: used in advanced automotive
L90@P0: control applications.
L91@P0: ADVANCED APPLICATIONS: VEHICLE DYNAMICS AND DRIVER ASSISTANCE SYSTEMS

L97@P0-1: Automotive Control SystemsThe first cars equipped with networking
L98@P1: capabilities based on the FlexRay protocol are
L99@P1: expected in 2006.
L100@P1: Freescale also offers its FlexRay implementation
L101@P1: to other semiconductor companies for license.
L102@P1: This licensing ensures that multiple vendors
L103@P1: offer interoperable solutions by making use of
L104@P1: the same FlexRay protocol core that conforms
L105@P1: to the FlexRay protocol specification.
L106@P1: Customer-specific product diversification
L107@P1: can be made at the host interface level.
L108@P1: FlexRay Advantages
L109@P1: > Backed by the majority of the automotive
L110@P1: industry, including the world’s three largest
L111@P1: volume car manufacturers
L112@P1: > Working prototype cars for system evaluation
L113@P1: in operation now
L114@P1: > Supported by a wide variety of tools available
L115@P1: from many development partners
L116@P1: > FPGA and silicon prototypes from Freescale
L117@P1: are available for key partners

L128@P1: Freescale’s Role in
L129@P1: the FlexRay Consortium
L130@P1: Freescale is adding its expertise to
L131@P1: the FlexRay initiative by codeveloping
L132@P1: the specifications for the automotive
L133@P1: data link layer. As for creating its own
L134@P1: FlexRay ready products, initially Freescale
L135@P1: will develop a FlexRay 2.0-compliant
L136@P1: module that can be used for license, standalone communications controllers and
L137@P1: integrated 16- and 32-bit microcontrollers.
L138@P1: Freescale uses the same FlexRay block for
L139@P1: all of its FlexRay products.
L140@P1: A single network protocol for automobiles
L141@P1: can help to speed the development
L142@P1: of system applications. It may also result in
L143@P1: cost savings as industry suppliers take
L144@P1: advantage of designing for a single platform
L145@P1: and the economies of scale of
L146@P1: manufacturing for one standard rather than
L147@P1: for many.
L148@P1: The FlexRay protocol was finalized in
L149@P1: July 2004. Freescale provided a field
L150@P1: programmable gate array (FPGA)
L151@P1: to DaimlerChrysler to display their first car
L152@P1: equipped with a FlexRay brake-by-wire
L153@P1: system in April 2002 at the first International
L154@P1: FlexRay Workshop in Munich, Germany.
L155@P1: Freescale provided the MFR4100, the
L156@P1: world’s first silicon chip of FlexRay, in
L157@P1: October 2003 to the consortium and its
L158@P1: members, with the FlexRay specification
L159@P1: version available at that time. Freescale
L160@P1: introduced the second FlexRay silicon chip
L161@P1: in May 2004 and a device, the MFR4200, is
L162@P1: expected to be qualified in the first half of
L163@P1: 2005 for production.
L164@P1: Freescale continues to drive FlexRay
L165@P1: Consortium activity to have a final reference
L166@P1: model and a conformance test in place to
L167@P1: ensure the interoperability of different
L168@P1: implementations of FlexRay on the market.
